outline: Measurement tools — run and control charts
diagnosis: Nonrandom shift on a run chart
mechanism: A run chart displays a measure in time order around a median. Run-chart rules are used to distinguish likely nonrandom change from ordinary variation. For a run chart with fewer than 20 data points, six or more consecutive points entirely above or below the median constitute a shift; points on the median are not counted. A shift is a signal that the underlying process may have changed and should be investigated in relation to interventions or other events.
vignette: An orthopedic service starts a standardized early-mobility protocol for patients undergoing uncomplicated total knee arthroplasty. The team tracks the weekly median number of hours from surgery to first ambulation on a run chart. The chart contains 16 weekly data points in total. A baseline median was established before the protocol. The first 6 weekly points after implementation are all below the baseline median; none lies on the median. The six values fluctuate up and down rather than decreasing steadily.
lead: Which of the following is the best interpretation of this run chart?
correct: The six consecutive points below the median constitute a nonrandom shift, suggesting that the care process changed after the intervention
distractors: The pattern is only common-cause variation because no control limits were crossed
The pattern is a downward trend because all six points are below the median
The protocol has been proven to cause the improvement because every post-intervention point is below the median
No conclusion about change can be drawn without a hypothesis test producing a p value below 0.05
distractor_notes: Run charts do not require control limits to identify nonrandom patterns. Control limits are a feature of control charts; run-chart rules use the median and the pattern of points over time.
A trend requires sequential points that continually increase or decrease. These six values fluctuate but remain on one side of the median, which is a shift rather than a trend.

A run-chart shift is evidence of a nonrandom change in the process, but temporal association alone does not prove that the intervention caused the change; other contemporaneous factors should still be considered.

Quality-improvement run charts are specifically designed to detect nonrandom patterns over time using run-chart rules. A conventional p-value hypothesis test is not required before recognizing a shift signal.
key_expl: This is a run-chart shift. IHI's run-chart rules define a shift as six or more consecutive points above or below the median when the chart contains fewer than 20 total data points, excluding points on the median. This chart has 16 points and six consecutive post-intervention observations below the baseline median, so it signals nonrandom change. Because the values are not steadily decreasing, the pattern is not a trend. The signal supports further interpretation of the process change but does not by itself prove causality.
objective: Interpret a quality-improvement run chart: with fewer than 20 total observations, six consecutive points on one side of the median constitute a nonrandom shift, whereas a trend requires sequential movement in one direction.
clues: six consecutive post-intervention points below median
values fluctuate rather than steadily decrease
